- When sentiment is consistently positive (≥0.67) over recent days, model tends to overestimate early in horizon; reduce initial forecast values.
- When sentiment is negative (≤0.33) or volatile, model underestimates sharp spikes; increase forecast for 1–3 days after sentiment turns positive.
- Model often overshoots after a spike in sentiment (e.g., 1.00), especially in 30-day horizon — cap forecast at 1.5x recent peak if sentiment was bullish.
- If sentiment history shows strong upward momentum (e.g., 3+ consecutive 1.00), model fails to capture mean reversion; reduce forecast by 15–30% in middle/late horizon.
- If sentiment is neutral (0.33–0.67) and price is rising, model underestimates continuation — add 0.1–0.3 to forecast for next 5–7 days.
- For 30-day forecasts, if true outcome shows >2x recent high, model often misses it — apply “lag correction”: if sentiment was bullish 3+ days ago, add 0.2–0.5 to forecast for day 10–15.
- If sentiment is negative and forecast is low, model often fails to recover — increase forecast by 0.1–0.3 for next 3–5 days if sentiment turns positive.
- Avoid overfitting to recent highs — if sentiment is bullish but price is flat, reduce forecast by 0.1–0.2 to avoid over-optimism.
